summary: Explains why the Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) was developed: to give retransmission-based reliability over links with very long round-trip times or frequent interruptions. Interplanetary communication is the main example. It is the first of a series of related documents, and it is informational.

eli5.summary: Sending a message to Mars takes minutes each way, so asking are you there is not practical. This explains why a special protocol is needed for such slow and unreliable trips.

subtitle: Why reliable transmission over deep-space links needs its own protocol instead of TCP.

tldr.problem: Terrestrial protocols like TCP assume short, predictable round-trip times and continuous connectivity. Interplanetary communication faces extreme delays (round-trip to Mars is 8+ minutes), long occultations (periods of no contact), and expensive bandwidth shared with other missions. TCP throughput becomes impractically low.
tldr.mechanism: LTP uses unidirectional sessions with explicit red-part (reliable) and green-part (best-effort) data, selective acknowledgments, no handshake, and adjustable timeout based on known light-time delays instead of statistical history.
tldr.outcome: LTP enables high-bandwidth reliable data transfer over deep-space links by tolerating extreme latencies and scheduling delays while avoiding TCP's unnecessary retransmissions.

today: RFC 5325 is an Experimental RFC documenting the motivation for LTP, the first of a series describing the Licklider Transmission Protocol. It has not been obsoleted and remains part of the Delay Tolerant Networking architecture for deep-space and delay-tolerant links.

sections.title: The Deep-Space Communication Environment
sections.content:
Interplanetary Internet (IPN) communication differs fundamentally from terrestrial networks. Signal propagation delay is the speed of light across space. The round-trip time from Earth to Europa (Jupiter's moon) ranges from 66 to 100 minutes. Even Mars, at closest approach, has an 8-minute one-way delay.

Occultation prevents communication when planets lose line-of-sight. During occultation, packets queue locally until connectivity resumes.

Intermittent scheduling adds further delay because NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN) is oversubscribed. Contact with a distant spacecraft must be carefully scheduled, and radio passes may be hours or days apart. This means packets can sit in a queue for weeks waiting for the next contact window.

These environmental constraints force a different approach to transport protocol design. Long delays mean round-trip times of minutes or hours (not milliseconds). Statistical estimates of RTT from history are meaningless when the next RTT could be orders of magnitude larger due to a contact window delay. Continuous connection cannot be assumed.
sections.eli5: Talking to a Mars rover is like sending a letter by mail: there is a weeks-long delay between when you mail it and when you get a reply. You can't stand around waiting for each answer before asking the next question.

sections.title: Why Not TCP or SCTP?
sections.content:
The RFC shows that TCP's throughput equation makes it impractical for deep space. Assuming an 8-minute round-trip to Mars, a 1500-byte packet, and acknowledgment of every other packet, achieving just 10 Kbps requires a loss rate of 4.68 × 10−6, and 1 Mbps would require an absurd 4.68 × 10−10 loss rate. Real deep-space links have much higher loss rates.

TCP's three-way handshake introduces delays of minutes or hours before data transmission can start. With an 8-minute RTT, a handshake alone wastes 24 minutes. TCP's congestion control (slow-start, exponential backoff) is designed for networks with short RTTs and causes severe throughput loss over long delays.

SCTP multiplexes multiple associations over one connection but still requires multiple round trips for setup before data flows, making it equally unsuitable.

Additionally, TCP connections are bidirectional, but deep-space missions typically use unidirectional data flows (commands are light, data from spacecraft is heavy) with separate links in each direction at different rates. TCP wastes bidirectional capacity.
sections.eli5: TCP keeps asking "got it?" after every couple of messages. In deep space, that's too slow. It also assumes you can talk two ways at the same speed, but we mostly listen to spacecraft reports.

sections.title: LTP's Design Approach
sections.content:
Unidirectional sessions: LTP transfers data in one direction only. Bidirectional communication uses two separate LTP sessions (one in each direction) with independent parameters, matching mission profiles.

Red and green parts: Each block of data is split into a red-part (reliable, must be acknowledged and retransmitted) and a green-part (best-effort, no retransmission). An application might send a header as red (essential) and payload as green (nice-to-have), or all-red or all-green as needed. There is no urgency hierarchy between them, just a reliability difference.

No negotiation: LTP parameters are asserted unilaterally, not negotiated via a handshake. This avoids the round-trip overhead of connection setup.

Stateful operation with selective reports: The receiver generates a reception report that details exactly which ranges of the red-part were received, allowing the sender to retransmit only missing pieces. This is more efficient than TCP's duplicate-acknowledgment approach.

Checkpoints and timers: Key segments are marked as checkpoints and trigger reception reports. The sender maintains a list of received ranges and retransmits what is missing. Timers are computed from known light-time delays, not from round-trip history, and are suspended during known occultation periods (communicated via "link state cues" from the operating environment).

Deferred transmission: Segments are queued for transmission at the next opportunity. Internal operation segments (reports, acknowledgments) have higher priority than application data, ensuring acknowledgments are sent promptly when the link becomes available.
sections.eli5: LTP sends a lot of data without waiting for replies, marking some as "must arrive" (red) and some as "best effort" (green). When the spacecraft finally sends a report saying what it received, we only resend the missing red parts.

sections.title: Nominal Session Flow
sections.content:
A client service asks LTP to transmit a block, specifying the remote destination, data location, total length, and the number of leading bytes to treat as red (reliable).

LTP segments the block into pieces, marks the last red-part segment with End of Red Part (EORP) and a checkpoint serial number. The last segment overall is marked End of Block (EOB). A timer is started for the EORP checkpoint.

When the link becomes active (signaled by a link state cue), the enqueued segments are transmitted to the receiver via the underlying data-link protocol. Receivers collect segments and, upon receiving the EORP segment, respond with a reception report listing all contiguous ranges of red-part data received.

The sender receives the report and sends a report-acknowledgment, turning off its checkpoint timer. If the reception report shows all red-part data was received, the sender notifies the client that the red-part transmission is complete. Upon reception of the report-acknowledgment, the receiver's session is complete.

If some red-part data is missing, the sender retransmits only those segments, marked with the report serial number as a checkpoint. The retransmission cycle continues until all red-part data is acknowledged. The green-part is delivered immediately upon receipt but is never retransmitted.
sections.eli5: Send: "Here are segments 1-100; tell me when you get them." Receive: "Got 1-50 and 75-100." Send: "Here are segments 51-74 again." Receive: "Got them all now." Done.

sections.title: Timer Calculation and Link State Cues
sections.content:
Expected arrival time for acknowledgment segments is computed from the known one-way light time (doubled for round trip), plus a small margin (typically 2 seconds) for processing and queuing, plus the delay due to occultation.

Link state cues from the operating environment inform LTP of which remote engines can currently receive transmissions and which can send. When connectivity is lost (e.g., during scheduled tracking pass end or occultation), LTP suspends the countdown timers for pending acknowledgments and resumes them when connectivity resumes, effectively adding the unavailability duration to the expected arrival time.

This approach avoids the error-prone task of inferring round-trip time from packet history and handles the fact that two consecutive segments might have vastly different RTTs if one is delayed by an occultation.

Reception reports may span multiple segments if many non-contiguous pieces were lost and the link MTU is small. LTP generates as many report segments as necessary, each covering a scope of red-part data and reporting received ranges within that scope.
sections.eli5: We know light takes 4 minutes to Mars, so we expect a reply 8+ minutes later. If we know Mars is in occultation (can't see Earth), we pause the timer until Mars rotates back into view.
